# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

## Optical Baseline and SAR Backscatter

The Sentinel-2-only models serve as the primary baseline for this thesis. Their test-set performance confirms the core finding of the preceding project work [@klaver2025]: pixel-based machine learning models using temporal differences in vegetation indices can detect mowing events with high accuracy when cloud-free imagery is available. The preceding study showed that even a single feature (ndii_diff) can achieve reasonable scene-level performance, and the refined feature selection in this thesis confirms that the mowing signal in optical data is concentrated in a small number of spectral change indicators. Reducing the feature set from five to three difference features produced a minimal drop in F1-Score (0.923 to 0.920), while retaining complementary spectral information (GNDVI, SWIR) stabilised predictions across varying scene conditions. This aligns with the broader observation by Garioud et al. [-@garioud2019] that simpler model configurations can be highly effective for mowing detection when training data is limited. The additional workflow improvements introduced in this thesis, including threshold calibration and postprocessing, are discussed in more detail below.

The GRD backscatter features showed negligible predictive value for mowing detection at this study site. The GRD-only configuration achieved near-random performance on the test set and failed completely at scene level, predicting nearly all grassland pixels as mowed (F1 around 0.200). Adding GRD features to the optical baseline did not improve test-set accuracy, and the operational scene-level results were similarly inconclusive, with S2+GRD performing comparably to or slightly below the S2-only configurations on most scenes. This outcome is consistent with the findings of De Vroey et al. [-@devroey2021], who reported that SAR backscatter alone is a weak predictor of mowing events due to the confounding influence of soil moisture, precipitation, and phenological variation on the returned amplitude signal. Reinermann et al. [-@reinermann2022] observed a similar pattern at larger scale: their integrated S1+S2 approach for Germany reduced the F1-Score from 0.65 to 0.61 compared to the optical-only method, with the degradation attributed to increased false positives from SAR features. While backscatter changes after mowing are physically expected, particularly a decrease in VH due to the loss of canopy volume scattering [@meyer2019], these changes appear to be small relative to the environmental noise floor at C-band frequencies and do not produce a reliable classification signal at the pixel level.

## Coherence Signal and Its Limitations

The integration of interferometric coherence derived from SLC data was motivated by the physical expectation that mowed grassland, presenting a more stable scattering surface, would produce measurably higher coherence than tall, moving vegetation. The seasonal coherence analysis (@tbl-coherence-seasonal) shows that this expectation is only partially supported at the Zurich Airport study site. A positive Cohen's $d$, corresponding to higher post-event coherence in mowed parcels, was observed exclusively for VH polarisation during the late growing season. VV polarisation produced near-zero effect sizes across all seasons, and both polarisations showed negative Cohen's $d$ values during the early and peak growing seasons.

These results are weaker than what the reference literature reports. Tamm et al. [-@tamm2016] found statistically significant coherence increases after mowing for both VH and VV polarisations, whereas at this study site only VH in the late season follows the expected pattern. De Vroey et al. [-@devroey2021] achieved a 54% event detection rate from coherence jumps in hay meadows, a result that, while modest, substantially exceeds the coherence-based detection capability observed here: the coherence-only models achieved F1-Scores of 0.468 to 0.479 on held-out test samples and dropped to approximately 0.200 at scene level, where the models predicted nearly all grassland pixels as mowed. The near-zero permutation importance of both coherence features (coh_vv, coh_vh) in the feature importance analysis further corroborates the weak pixel-level signal.

Several factors likely contribute to this discrepancy. First, the airport grasslands are managed under specific operational protocols that differ from the agricultural grasslands studied by Tamm et al. [-@tamm2016] and De Vroey et al. [-@devroey2021], with potentially different grass species, cutting heights, and mowing frequencies. Notably, the airport site does not involve grazing, which De Vroey et al. [-@devroey2021] identified as a major source of false detections in their study. The absence of this confounding factor should theoretically improve coherence-based detection, yet performance remains poor. Second, the Sentinel-1 repeat cycle of 6 or 12 days means that rapid regrowth during the peak season can substantially reduce the coherence contrast between mowed and unmowed areas before the second acquisition of a pair is recorded. This aligns with the finding of Tamm et al. [-@tamm2016] that the 12-day temporal baseline proved insufficient during rapid growth phases, and may partly explain the inverted signal observed during the early and peak seasons. Third, the C-band wavelength of 5.6 cm interacts with vegetation at a scale where even short grass stubble may still produce appreciable volume scattering [@meyer2019], reducing the expected coherence increase.

The SNR correction following Tamm et al. [-@tamm2016] consistently improved the statistical separability of the classes by increasing the magnitude of Cohen's $d$ and lowering p-values across most season and polarisation combinations. However, the correction amplified existing signals without reversing the sign of the effect in any configuration, leaving the fundamental signal weakness unresolved.

These pixel-level findings explain why the coherence-only models achieved near-random F1-Scores in both training evaluation and operational application. While the seasonal analysis demonstrates that a coherence signal exists at the parcel level in late season, the per-pixel variability is too high for a pixel-based classifier to exploit reliably. A parcel-level or segment-based approach, where coherence is averaged over predefined spatial units, could potentially yield better class separability, but would sacrifice the ability to detect sub-parcel mowing patterns, which is a relevant use case at the airport where mowing frequently affects only portions of larger grassland areas.

Despite these limitations, including coherence features alongside optical features in the Full-fusion RF produced the highest test-set F1-Score within Group B (0.922) and competitive operational results. This suggests that the classifier can extract some complementary information from coherence that is not captured by optical indices alone, even when the standalone signal is weak. The selective integration strategy, informed by permutation importance analysis, proved essential: adding all available features indiscriminately degraded performance for some classifiers, particularly the SVM.

An additional factor that may contribute to the weak pixel-level coherence signal is the resolution mismatch between the optical and SAR features. The coherence rasters were computed at 20 m and resampled to the 10 m optical grid using bilinear interpolation, meaning that each original coherence pixel covers four optical pixels. At parcel boundaries, where mowed and unmowed areas meet, this resampling produces blended coherence values that do not correspond to either class. For a pixel-based classifier operating at 10 m resolution, these mixed boundary pixels add noise to the coherence features without carrying discriminative information. This effect is difficult to separate from the inherent weakness of the C-band coherence signal at this site, but it likely contributes to the poor pixel-level class separability, particularly for smaller mowing events.


## Operational Improvements and Model Stability

The scene-level threshold calibration emerged as the single most impactful operational improvement in this thesis. The calibrated thresholds for S2-based models ranged from 0.775 to 0.950, far above the default of 0.5, reflecting the severe class imbalance at scene level where typically less than 10% of grassland pixels are mowed at any given time. On scene 46, threshold calibration alone improved the F1-Score from 0.477 to 0.587, primarily by increasing precision from 0.327 to 0.499 while recall decreased moderately from 0.881 to 0.712 (@fig-threshold-calibration).

This improvement has direct implications for interpreting the postprocessing results. Spatial postprocessing methods such as morphological filtering target isolated false positive pixels [@blaschke2010], the same type of noise that threshold calibration addresses at the decision level. Because the calibrated threshold already eliminates the majority of scattered false detections, the residual noise available for postprocessing is limited. This explains why the best postprocessing configuration achieved only a marginal mean improvement of +0.009 F1 over the calibrated baseline, and why the effect was inconsistent across scenes (@fig-pp-f1-comparison). In early experiments using models from the preceding study [@klaver2025] without threshold calibration, postprocessing produced substantially larger improvements, confirming that the two mechanisms target the same error source. The poor performance of SLIC-based postprocessing (F1 dropping to approximately 0.235) further illustrates this point: at the tested parameter ranges, mowing events at this site often affect areas that are small relative to the superpixel segment size, causing the mowed pixels to be outvoted by the surrounding unmowed majority during aggregation.

Despite the overall improvements in classification performance, no single model configuration performed consistently best across scenes. On scene 12, the S2-only_diff SVM achieved the highest F1-Score, while on scene 73, the S2-only_best RF performed best. The Full-fusion RF ranked third on both scenes but was never the top performer. This instability extends to the feature importance analysis, where individual feature rankings shifted substantially between Group A and Group B. The limited number of training events (63 for Group A, 24 for Group B) means that the specific composition of each group can disproportionately influence both feature importance estimates and model performance. Scene-level evaluation amplifies this effect, as each scene represents a single spatial and temporal snapshot with its own weather conditions, mowing patterns, and ground truth quality. A further source of uncertainty lies in the ground truth data itself, which were recorded by hand and subsequently digitised, a process in which spatial accuracy can be lost at both stages. Occasional inconsistencies between model predictions and ground truth labels suggest that some mowing events may have been incompletely recorded, meaning that reported performance likely represents a conservative estimate for certain scenes.

Taken together, the enhanced workflow substantially improves upon the baseline from the preceding project work [@klaver2025]. On scene 73, the best current model (S2-only_best RF, F1 = 0.749) nearly doubles the F1-Score of the PW2 model (F1 = 0.397). On scene 12, the improvement is smaller but consistent (0.689 vs 0.597). In both cases, the improvement is driven primarily by precision, reflecting the combined effect of the expanded multi-feature design, which captures the mowing signal more robustly than a single vegetation index, and the scene-level threshold calibration, which adapts the decision boundary to the actual class distribution encountered during application. The salt-and-pepper noise [@blaschke2010] that characterised the PW2 predictions is substantially reduced, and the models produce spatially more coherent predictions that better correspond to the expected shapes of mowing events. However, the variability across scenes means that the choice of model configuration for operational deployment should be based on average performance across multiple scenes rather than on any single evaluation. The S2-only configurations offer the most consistent performance with the least data dependency, making them the most robust choice for deployment at this stage.

The generalisation test near Lindau provides further evidence that the workflow transfers beyond the training site. Although the reported F1-Score of 0.516 is low, this is largely attributable to incomplete ground truth coverage: only four parcels from a single provider were available for evaluation, while the surrounding area contains numerous additional grassland parcels. Visual comparison of the before and after RGB composites shows that many of the areas flagged as false positives display clear spectral changes consistent with vegetation removal, and the predicted mowing areas form spatially coherent parcel-shaped regions rather than scattered noise. Importantly, the model was applied without a grassland mask over the full scene extent, yet did not produce false detections on forests, roads, buildings, or bare soil. This suggests that the spectral change features are sufficiently specific to grassland vegetation dynamics that a land cover mask, while useful for reducing computation, is not required to prevent systematic misclassification of non-vegetated surfaces.

## Limitations

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the results of this study.

The model was trained and evaluated exclusively on grasslands at Zurich Airport. Airport grasslands are managed under specific operational protocols and may not be representative of agricultural or ecological grassland management in other regions. The extent to which the model generalises to other sites, grass species, and management regimes remains largely untested.

The ground truth data, recorded by hand and subsequently digitised, represent the single primary reference source for this study. Despite substantial efforts to acquire additional ground truth from external institutions, no datasets with the required spatial and temporal resolution were obtained in sufficient quantity. The limited spatial precision of these records directly affects both model training and evaluation, and the absence of independent reference data means that the reported performance metrics cannot be validated against a second source.

The generalisation test near Lindau provides only a preliminary indication of spatial transferability. The reference data covers just four mowing polygons from a single provider, and mowing events on surrounding parcels managed by other farmers are not documented. Visual comparison of the before and after RGB composites confirms that several areas flagged as false positives show spectral changes consistent with vegetation removal, suggesting that the reported F1-Score of 0.516 represents a lower bound on actual performance at this site. A meaningful assessment of generalisation would require comprehensive ground truth across the full evaluation area.

The coherence features were available for only 24 of the 63 training events. This reduction results from two factors: the strict temporal matching requirements of the quadruplet design, and silent processing failures in SNAP that produced invalid zero-value outputs for half of the matched SLC pairs. The reduced sample size for Group B configurations limits statistical power and means that the comparison between S2-only and S2+coherence models operates on different subsets of the data with different event compositions.

The coherence rasters were computed at 20 m resolution and resampled to 10 m to match the optical grid. This resampling introduces spatial smoothing and means that the coherence features do not capture sub-20 m spatial variability. The mismatch in native resolution between the optical and SAR features is a structural limitation of combining these two sensor types.

The current coherence feature design uses only absolute coherence values (coh_vv, coh_vh) from the pre-mowing and post-mowing pairs. Computing a coherence temporal difference analogous to the optical feature design would require six SLC acquisitions per event rather than four, further reducing the number of usable training events and was therefore not pursued. Given the weak pixel-level coherence signal observed at this site, it is uncertain whether the additional temporal information would have produced meaningful improvement.

## Conclusion and Outlook

This thesis investigated whether the integration of SAR interferometric coherence and spatial postprocessing methods can improve automated mowing detection from satellite imagery. The findings can be summarised with respect to the research questions posed in @sec-introduction.

Regarding the integration of SAR data (Q1): GRD backscatter provided no useful signal for mowing detection. Interferometric coherence showed a physically meaningful but weak and season-dependent response that could not support standalone detection. When selectively combined with optical features, coherence contributed marginal improvements on balanced test sets, but this advantage did not consistently translate to operational scene-level application. The goal of reducing dependence on cloud-free optical acquisitions through SAR data was therefore not achieved in a practically meaningful way.

Regarding spatial postprocessing (Q2): morphological filtering and median pre-filtering produced small, inconsistent improvements in classification F1-Score. The limited impact is attributable to the effectiveness of scene-level threshold calibration, which addresses the same false positive noise that postprocessing targets. SLIC superpixel aggregation degraded performance at the tested parameter ranges.

Regarding ground truth acquisition (Q3): extensive efforts to obtain additional reference data from external institutions were unsuccessful, confirming that the availability of spatially precise mowing records remains the primary bottleneck for scaling and validating mowing detection workflows.

Regarding the comparison with the PW2 baseline (Q4): the enhanced workflow substantially improves upon the baseline, nearly doubling the operational F1-Score on one evaluation scene. The improvement is driven by the multi-feature design and the scene-level threshold calibration rather than by the addition of SAR data.

For future work, the most impactful direction would be the acquisition of diverse, spatially precise ground truth data across multiple sites and management regimes. This would enable both robust model validation and the investigation of transferability. For coherence specifically, a parcel-level or segment-based classification approach, where coherence is spatially averaged before classification, could yield better results than the pixel-based approach pursued here, though at the cost of losing sub-parcel spatial resolution. Additionally, computing coherence temporal differences from six-acquisition sequences could provide stronger features, if sufficient SLC data availability can be ensured. The generalisation test demonstrated that the model avoids systematic false detections on non-grassland surfaces even without a land cover mask, which is encouraging for operational deployment in areas where prior land use data is unavailable. Finally, evaluating the operational workflow across a broader range of scenes and years would provide the statistical basis needed to identify a reliably optimal model configuration for deployment.
